↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). IRRIGATION As streams were few in Palestine, water was generally stored up in winter in reservoirs, and distributed through gardens in numerous rills, which could easily be turned or diverted by the foot (Deuteronomy 11:10). For purposes of irrigation, water was raised from streams or pools by water-wheels, or by a shaduf, commonly used on the banks of the Nile to the present day.

↩ ◇ Note. Tefillin and mezuzah. This verse, together with 6:8–9, is the textual basis for two enduring practices: tefillin (small leather boxes containing scripture passages, bound to head and arm during morning prayer) and mezuzah (a parchment scroll affixed to doorposts). Tefillin from the Second Temple period have been recovered at Qumran. The tradition reads the metaphor literally; some Christian and modern Jewish traditions read it figuratively. Both readings have ancient pedigrees.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). DEBT The Mosaic law encouraged the practice of lending (Deuteronomy 15:7; Psalm 37:26; Matthew 5:42); but it forbade the exaction of interest except from foreigners. Usury was strongly condemned (Proverbs 28:8; Ezekiel 18:8, 13, 17; 22:12; Psalm 15:5). On the Sabbatical year all pecuniary obligations were cancelled (Deuteronomy 15:1-11). These regulations prevented the accumulation of debt.

↩ ◇ Note. The realism of poverty. Verse 11 sits in tension with v. 4 (“there shall be no poor among you”) — the same chapter holds out both the ideal and the realistic acknowledgment. The resolution: poverty is not inevitable in principle (if the Sabbatical-year debt release is observed), but inevitable in practice (because it won’t be). Jesus alludes to this verse in Mark 14:7 — not to dismiss the poor but to invoke the whole context: the perpetual obligation that follows from their perpetual presence.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). STEPHEN one of the seven deacons, who became a preacher of the gospel. He was the first Christian martyr. His personal character and history are recorded in Acts 6. “He fell asleep” with a prayer for his persecutors on his lips (7:60). Devout men carried him to his grave (8:2). It was at the feet of the young Pharisee, Saul of Tarsus, that those who stoned him laid their clothes (comp. Deuteronomy 17:5-7) before they began their cruel work. The scene which Saul then witnessed and the words he heard appear to have made a deep and lasting impression on his mind (Acts 22:19, 20). The speech of Stephen before the Jewish ruler is the first apology for the universalism of the gospel as a message to the Gentiles as well as the Jews. It is the longest speech contained in the Acts, a place of prominence being given to it as a defence.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). WITNESS More than one witness was required in criminal cases (Deuteronomy 17:6; 19:15). They were the first to execute the sentence on the condemned (Deuteronomy 13:9; 17:7; 1 Kings 21:13; Matthew 27:1; Acts 7:57, 58). False witnesses were liable to punishment (Deuteronomy 19:16-21). It was also an offence to refuse to bear witness (Leviticus 5:1).

↩ ⌘ Hebrew. Mishneh ha-torah (מִשְׁנֵה הַתּוֹרָה). The phrase that the LXX rendered as Deuteronomion — “second law” — and that gave the book its Greek and English name. The Hebrew actually means “a copy of this law,” and refers specifically to the personal scroll a king must write for himself and read all his days (17:18–20). The intent: even the king is under Torah, must read it daily, must not lift himself above his fellow-Israelites. One of the most striking limitations on royal power in the ancient Near East.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). DIVINATION of false prophets (Deuteronomy 18:10, 14; Micah 3:6, 7, 11), of necromancers (1 Samuel 28:8), of the Philistine priests and diviners (1 Samuel 6:2), of Balaam (Joshua 13:22). Three kinds of divination are mentioned in Ezekiel 21:21, by arrows, consulting with images (the teraphim), and by examining the entrails of animals sacrificed. The practice of this art seems to have been encouraged in ancient Egypt. Diviners also abounded among the aborigines of Canaan and the Philistines (Isaiah 2:6; 1 Samuel 28). At a later period multitudes of magicians poured from Chaldea and Arabia into the land of Israel, and pursued their occupations (Isaiah 8:19; 2 Kings 21:6; 2 Chronicles 33:6). This superstition widely spread, and in the time of the apostles there were “vagabond Jews, exorcists” (Acts 19:13), and men like Simon Magus (Acts 8:9), Bar-Jesus (13:6, 8), and other jugglers and impostors (19:19; 2 Timothy 3:13). Every species and degree of this superstition was strictly forbidden by the law of Moses (Exodus 22:18; Leviticus 19:26, 31; 20:27; Deuteronomy 18:10, 11). But beyond these various forms of superstition, there are instances of divination on record in the Scriptures by which God was pleased to make known his will. (1.) There was divination by lot, by which, when resorted to in matters of moment, and with solemnity, God intimated his will (Joshua 7:13). The land of Canaan was divided by lot (Numbers 26:55, 56); Achan’s guilt was detected (Joshua 7:16-19), Saul was elected king (1 Samuel 10:20, 21), and Matthias chosen to the apostleship, by the solem lot (Acts 1:26). It was thus also that the scape-goat was determined (Leviticus 16:8-10). (2.) There was divination by dreams (Genesis 20:6; Deuteronomy 13:1, 3; Judges 7:13, 15; Matthew 1:20; 2:12, 13, 19, 22). This is illustrated in the history of Joseph (Genesis 41:25-32) and of Daniel (2:27; 4:19-28). (3.) By divine appointment there was also divination by the Urim and Thummim (Numbers 27:21), and by the ephod. (4.) God was pleased sometimes to vouch-safe direct vocal communications to men (Deuteronomy 34:10; Exodus 3:4; 4:3; Deuteronomy 4:14, 15; 1 Kings 19:12). He also communed with men from above the mercy-seat (Exodus 25:22), and at the door of the tabernacle (Exodus 29:42, 43). (5.) Through his prophets God revealed himself, and gave intimations of his will (2 Kings 13:17; Jeremiah 51:63, 64).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). FAMILIAR SPIRIT Sorcerers or necormancers, who professed to call up the dead to answer questions, were said to have a “familiar spirit” (Deuteronomy 18:11; 2 Kings 21:6; 2 Chronicles 33:6; Leviticus 19:31; 20:6; Isaiah 8:19; 29:4). Such a person was called by the Hebrews an ’ob, which properly means a leathern bottle; for sorcerers were regarded as vessels containing the inspiring demon. This Hebrew word was equivalent to the pytho of the Greeks, and was used to denote both the person and the spirit which possessed him (Leviticus 20:27; 1 Samuel 28:8; comp. Acts 16:16). The word “familiar” is from the Latin familiaris, meaning a “household servant,” and was intended to express the idea that sorcerers had spirits as their servants ready to obey their commands.

↩ ◇ Note. The prophet like Moses. A foundational messianic text in Second Temple Judaism. Read variously as Joshua, the prophetic line as a whole, or a specific eschatological figure. Acts 3:22 and 7:37 apply it to Jesus; the Samaritan tradition applies it to the Taheb; the Qumran community to a coming prophet alongside two messiahs. The verse marks Israel’s transition from direct theophany at Sinai (which the people couldn’t bear, 18:16) to mediated prophecy — and the long expectation of one prophet who would speak with Mosaic immediacy again.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). FIRST-BORN sons enjoyed certain special privileges (Deuteronomy 21:17; Genesis 25:23, 31, 34; 49:3; 1 Chronicles 5:1; Hebrews 12:16; Psalm 89:27). (See BIRTHRIGHT.) The “first-born of the poor” signifies the most miserable of the poor (Isaiah 14:30). The “church of the first-born” signifies the church of the redeemed. The destruction of the first-born was the last of the ten plagues inflicted on the Egyptians (Exodus 11:1-8; 12:29, 30). Menephtah is probably the Pharaoh whose first-born was slain. His son did not succeed or survive his father, but died early. The son’s tomb has been found at Thebes unfinished, showing it was needed earlier than was expected. Some of the records on the tomb are as follows: “The son whom Menephtah loves; who draws towards him his father’s heart, the singer, the prince of archers, who governed Egypt on behalf of his father. Dead.”

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). APPAREL In Old Testament times the distinction between male and female attire was not very marked. The statute forbidding men to wear female apparel (Deuteronomy 22:5) referred especially to ornaments and head-dresses. Both men and women wore (1) an under garment or tunic, which was bound by a girdle. One who had only this tunic on was spoken of as “naked” (1 Samuel 19:24; Job 24:10; Isaiah 20:2). Those in high stations sometimes wore two tunics, the outer being called the “upper garment” (1 Samuel 15:27; 18:4; 24:5; Job 1:20). (2.) They wore in common an over-garment (“mantle,” Isaiah 3:22; 1 Kings 19:13; 2 Kings 2:13), a loose and flowing robe. The folds of this upper garment could be formed into a lap (Ruth 3:15; Psalm 79:12; Proverbs 17:23; Luke 6:38). Generals of armies usually wore scarlet robes (Judges 8:26; Nah. 2:3). A form of conspicuous raiment is mentioned in Luke 20:46; comp. Matthew 23:5. Priests alone wore trousers. Both men and women wore turbans. Kings and nobles usually had a store of costly garments for festive occasions (Isaiah 3:22; Zechariah 3:4) and for presents (Genesis 45:22; Esther 4:4; 6:8, 11; 1 Samuel 18:4; 2 Kings 5:5; 10:22). Prophets and ascetics wore coarse garments (Isaiah 20:2; Zechariah 13:4; Matthew 3:4).

↩ ◇ Note. Tzitzit, Deuteronomic version. Numbers 15:38 introduced the tassels with the blue thread; Deuteronomy here adds the requirement of four corners explicitly — and prepares the way for the four-cornered prayer shawl (tallit) that would emerge in the rabbinic period. The practice is one of the most visible threads of continuity between biblical Israel and contemporary Judaism. The garment Jesus wears in the Gospels — whose hem the bleeding woman touches — was a four-cornered tasseled cloak.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). BASTARD In the Old Testament the rendering of the Hebrew word mamzer’, which means “polluted.” In Deuteronomy 23:2, it occurs in the ordinary sense of illegitimate offspring. In Zechariah 9:6, the word is used in the sense of foreigner. From the history of Jephthah we learn that there were bastard offspring among the Jews (Judges 11:1-7). In Hebrews 12:8, the word (Gr. nothoi) is used in its ordinary sense, and denotes those who do not share the privileges of God’s children.

↩ ✦ Topic. Topics. This verse appears under: Children, Church of Israel.

↩ ◇ Note. The exclusion clause. Read straightforwardly, this verse permanently bars Moabites from the assembly of Yahweh — yet the Book of Ruth tells the story of a Moabite woman who becomes the great-grandmother of King David. Already within the Hebrew Bible, the rule and its great exception sit side by side. The rabbis later distinguished “Moabite (man)” from “Moabite woman,” preserving Ruth’s standing. The passage became a flashpoint in post-exilic readings (Nehemiah 13:1–3) and a model of how the canon contains its own internal critiques.

↩ ◇ Note. Ox and apostle. Paul cites this verse twice to argue that ministers of the gospel deserve material support (1 Cor 9:9, 1 Tim 5:18). His move is hermeneutically aggressive: he calls the surface meaning insufficient (“is it for oxen that God is concerned?”) and reads the rule as analogically about workers’ wages. Whatever one thinks of the move, it is a clear case of the New Testament reading the Torah typologically — the ox’s right to eat as it works becomes a paradigm for the worker’s right to wages.

↩ ◇ Ephrem the Syrian (365). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Deuteronomy (c. 365 AD)

On 'Thou shalt not muzzle the ox when he treadeth out the corn' (Deu 25:4), Ephrem reads the agricultural-mercy statute as the canonical Old-Testament anchor of Paul's argument for ministerial support: cited at 1 Cor 9:9 and 1 Tim 5:18 with the gloss 'Doth God take care for oxen? or saith he it altogether for our sakes? For our sakes, no doubt, this is written.' The verse becomes the apostolic warrant for the priest's right to be sustained by the eucharistic offerings of the people. Tewahedo canonical-economy cites Deu 25:4 + 1 Cor 9:9 as the canonical doubled-witness for the lay-support of the priest and the monastery — the worker is worthy of his hire.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). MUZZLE Grain in the East is usually thrashed by the sheaves being spread out on a floor, over which oxen and cattle are driven to and fro, till the grain is trodden out. Moses ordained that the ox was not to be muzzled while thrashing. It was to be allowed to eat both the grain and the straw (Deuteronomy 25:4). (See AGRICULTURE.)

↩ ◇ Note. Remember Amalek. A unique commandment: to remember what Amalek did, in order to blot out his memory (vv. 17, 19). The paradox is built into the text. In synagogue practice, the passage is read on the Sabbath before Purim (the festival of Esther, who descended from Saul, the king commanded to destroy Amalek’s descendant Agag in 1 Sam 15). “Amalek” in later Jewish thought becomes a cipher for civilizational evil — a category, not just a tribe.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). EBAL stony. (1.) A mountain 3,076 feet above the level of the sea, and 1,200 feet above the level of the valley, on the north side of which stood the city of Shechem (q.v.). On this mountain six of the tribes (Deuteronomy 27:12,13) were appointed to take their stand and respond according to a prescribed form to the imprecations uttered in the valley, where the law was read by the Levites (11:29; 29:4, 13). This mountain was also the site of the first great altar erected to Jehovah (Deuteronomy 27:5-8; Joshua 8:30-35). After this the name of Ebal does not again occur in Jewish history. (See GERIZIM.) (2.) A descendant of Eber (1 Chronicles 1:22), called also Obal (Genesis 10:28). (3.) A descendant of Seir the Horite (Genesis 36:23).

↩ ◇ Note. The covenant ceremony at Ebal and Gerizim. Six tribes on Mount Gerizim recite blessings, six on Mount Ebal recite curses; the Levites speak the formal liturgy in the valley between. Twelve curses, each answered by a public “Amen.” The setting is geographically dramatic — Gerizim and Ebal still stand in the West Bank as facing peaks above modern Nablus. The Samaritan community (whose temple stood on Gerizim) reads the order of mountains differently, with Gerizim as the mountain of blessing and the primary cult site — a textual variant traceable back to manuscripts like the Samaritan Pentateuch.

↩ ◇ Note. The blessings. The blessings (28:1–14) are the shorter half of the covenant ratification. Note the rhetorical pattern: the chapter front-loads the blessings briefly and dwells extensively on the curses (vv. 15–68 — more than three times as long) — a classic ancient Near Eastern treaty pattern, designed to terrify the vassal into compliance. The book of Lamentations reads as a sustained meditation on the curses’ fulfillment.

↩ ◇ Note. The covenant curses. The longest list of covenant curses in the Bible — and one of the most rhetorically intense passages in all of scripture. The escalating intensity (siege, cannibalism, exile, dispersion) parallels Hittite and Assyrian treaty curses of the second and first millennia BCE. The closing image — Israel being sold back into Egypt as slaves and finding no buyer (28:68) — completes a tragic frame: the people who came out of Egyptian slavery returning to it.

↩ ◇ Note. Other lands, other peoples. Deuteronomy 2 distinguishes Israel’s land-grant from those of neighboring peoples — Edom (Esau), Moab (Lot), Ammon (Lot) — each given their own territory by Yahweh, off-limits to Israelite conquest. The theological move is significant: Yahweh is portrayed as the universal allotter of lands, not merely Israel’s tribal deity. Compare Deut 32:8, where Yahweh sets the boundaries of all peoples. The chapter is an early articulation of what Christian theologians later call common providence.

↩ ◇ Ephrem the Syrian (365). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Deuteronomy (c. 365 AD)

On 'And thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thine heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy might' (Deu 6:5), Ephrem reads the threefold-totality of love as the canonical Old-Testament anchor of the Great Commandment that Christ cites as 'the first and great commandment' (Mt 22:37-38). Heart, soul, might: nothing of the human person is exempt from the demand. Tewahedo monastic theology cites Deu 6:5 + Mt 22:37 as the canonical doubled-witness that monastic poverty (yielding might), monastic chastity (yielding heart), and monastic obedience (yielding soul) are the threefold practical realization of the one Shema-commandment.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). HEART According to the Bible, the heart is the centre not only of spiritual activity, but of all the operations of human life. “Heart” and “soul” are often used interchangeably (Deuteronomy 6:5; 26:16; comp. Matthew 22:37; Mark 12:30, 33), but this is not generally the case. The heart is the “home of the personal life,” and hence a man is designated, according to his heart, wise (1 Kings 3:12, etc.), pure (Psalm 24:4; Matthew 5:8, etc.), upright and righteous (Genesis 20:5, 6; Psalm 11:2; 78:72), pious and good (Luke 8:15), etc. In these and such passages the word “soul” could not be substituted for “heart.” The heart is also the seat of the conscience (Romans 2:15). It is naturally wicked (Genesis 8:21), and hence it contaminates the whole life and character (Matthew 12:34; 15:18; comp. Ecclesiastes 8:11; Psalm 73:7). Hence the heart must be changed, regenerated (Ezekiel 36:26; 11:19; Psalm 51:10-14), before a man can willingly obey God. The process of salvation begins in the heart by the believing reception of the testimony of God, while the rejection of that testimony hardens the heart (Psalm 95:8; Proverbs 28:14; 2 Chronicles 36:13). “Hardness of heart evidences itself by light views of sin; partial acknowledgment and confession of it; pride and conceit; ingratitude; unconcern about the word and ordinances of God; inattention to divine providences; stifling convictions of conscience; shunning reproof; presumption, and general ignorance of divine things.”

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). DOOR-POSTS The Jews were commanded to write the divine name on the posts (mezuzoth’) of their doors (Deuteronomy 6:9). ↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). BUILDING among the Jews was suited to the climate and conditions of the country. They probably adopted the kind of architecture for their dwellings which they found already existing when they entered Canaan (Deuteronomy 6:10; Numbers 13:19). Phoenician artists (2 Samuel 5:11; 1 Kings 5:6, 18) assisted at the erection of the royal palace and the temple at Jerusalem. Foreigners also assisted at the restoration of the temple after the Exile (Ezra 3:7). In Genesis 11:3, 9, we have the first recorded instance of the erection of buildings. The cities of the plain of Shinar were founded by the descendants of Shem (10:11, 12, 22). The Israelites were by occupation shepherds and dwellers in tents (Genesis 47:3); but from the time of their entering Canaan they became dwellers in towns, and in houses built of the native limestone of Palestine. Much building was carried on in Solomon’s time. Besides the buildings he completed at Jerusalem, he also built Baalath and Tadmor (1 Kings 9:15, 24). Many of the kings of Israel and Judah were engaged in erecting various buildings. Herod and his sons and successors restored the temple, and built fortifications and other structures of great magnificence in Jerusalem (Luke 21:5). The instruments used in building are mentioned as the plumb-line (Amos 7:7), the measuring-reed (Ezekiel 40:3), and the saw (1 Kings 7:9). Believers are “God’s building” (1 Corinthians 3:9); and heaven is called “a building of God” (2 Corinthians 5:1). Christ is the only foundation of his church (1 Corinthians 3:10-12), of which he also is the builder (Matthew 16:18).

↩ ◇ Ephrem the Syrian (365). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Deuteronomy (c. 365 AD)

On 'Thou shalt fear the Lord thy God, and serve him' (Deu 6:13), Ephrem reads the doubled-verb (fear + serve) as the canonical Old-Testament anchor invoked by Christ at the third Temptation: 'Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and him only shalt thou serve' (Mt 4:10). The Septuagint's substitution of 'worship' (proskunēseis) for 'fear' (phobēthēsē) preserves the doubled-verb structure that Christ retains. Tewahedo christology cites Deu 6:13 + Mt 4:10 as the canonical doubled-witness that Christ in his humanity submits to the Father-alone-worshipped, providing the typological model for every Tewahedo refusal of demonic or imperial worship.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). OATH a solemn appeal to God, permitted on fitting occasions (Deuteronomy 6:13; Jeremiah 4:2), in various forms (Genesis 16:5; 2 Samuel 12:5; Ruth 1:17; Hos. 4:15; Romans 1:9), and taken in different ways (Genesis 14:22; 24:2; 2 Chronicles 6:22). God is represented as taking an oath (Hebrews 6:16-18), so also Christ (Matthew 26:64), and Paul (Romans 9:1; Galatians 1:20; Phil. 1:8). The precept, “Swear not at all,” refers probably to ordinary conversation between man and man (Matthew 5:34,37). But if the words are taken as referring to oaths, then their intention may have been to show “that the proper state of Christians is to require no oaths; that when evil is expelled from among them every yea and nay will be as decisive as an oath, every promise as binding as a vow.”

↩ ◇ Note. Massah. The location of the water-from-rock incident in Exod 17:1–7, where Israel disputed (rib) and tested (nasah) Yahweh — hence the place-names Massah and Meribah. Jesus quotes this verse to the tempter in the wilderness (Matt 4:7, Luke 4:12) — refusing to put God to the test. The verse becomes one of the most-cited NT proof-texts for the spiritual posture of trust without sign-demand.

↩ ◇ Note. The seven nations. The list (Hittite, Girgashite, Amorite, Canaanite, Perizzite, Hivite, Jebusite) recurs in slight variations a dozen times across the Hexateuch. Recent scholarship reads the list less as a population census than as a theological cipher: the "seven" is a literary fullness number, and several of the named groups (Hittites, Hivites) were not present in the land in the form the text describes. The list’s function is to frame the conquest as confronting completed Canaanite cultural-religious systems, not specific tribes.

↩ ◇ Note. Gerizim and Ebal. The two peaks above Shechem (modern Nablus) — Gerizim to the south (the blessing mountain, lush) and Ebal to the north (the curse mountain, barer). The Samaritan community has worshiped on Mount Gerizim continuously for ~2,500 years; the John 4 conversation between Jesus and the Samaritan woman ("our fathers worshiped on this mountain") refers to it. The Samaritan Pentateuch reads Gerizim where MT reads Ebal in some passages — one of the major textual dividing lines between the two Pentateuch traditions.

↩ ◇ Note. The false-prophet test. Even genuine signs and wonders do not legitimize a prophet who calls Israel to other gods (13:2–3). The criterion is theological, not phenomenological: by what god is the prophet calling you to live? The principle is essential to the canon’s self-policing — Israelite prophecy never validates itself by miracle alone. The same logic underlies 1 Cor 12:3 and Gal 1:8 in the New Testament.

↩ ◇ Ephrem the Syrian (365). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Deuteronomy (c. 365 AD)

On the Deuteronomic recapitulation of Passover — 'Observe the month of Abib, and keep the passover unto the Lord thy God' (Deu 16:1) — Ephrem reads the THIRD Mosaic Passover legislation (after Exo 12 and Num 9) as the canonical triple-witness that Pascha is the non-negotiable hinge of the covenant year. The repetition is not redundant but emphatic: the Lord wills that Israel never forget the month of deliverance. Tewahedo Fasika theology cites Exo 12 + Num 9:2 + Deu 16:1 as the canonical triple-Mosaic anchor that the yearly Pascha is constitutive of covenant identity — eucharistically fulfilled in the Tewahedo Holy-Week Anaphora.

The phrase that names the matzah of Passover. ‘Oni means both "affliction" and "humiliation, lowliness" — the bread is poor man’s bread because it is the bread of haste, of slavery’s end, of unleavened time. The Passover Haggadah uses precisely this phrase as the opening line of Ha Lachma Anya, the invitation that begins the seder: "This is the bread of affliction our ancestors ate in the land of Egypt."

↩ ◇ Note. The peace-offer protocol. Before besieging a distant city, Israel must offer terms. If accepted, the population becomes tribute-paying laborers (20:11); if refused, full siege follows. The chapter goes on to exempt cities of the seven Canaanite nations from this protocol (20:16–18), which has troubled readers since antiquity. The internal tension between the universal peace-offer and the local ḥerem is the Bible’s own awkwardness with its conquest theology, not a modern complaint imposed on it.

↩ ◇ Note. The bill of divorce. Deuteronomy 24:1–4 was a foundational legal text in Second Temple debates about divorce — the schools of Hillel and Shammai argued at length over what counts as ‘ervat davar ("indecency, unseemly thing"). Jesus engages this exact debate in Matt 19:3–9 / Mark 10:2–12, taking a stricter line than even Shammai. The mechanism here protects a divorced woman from being reclaimed by her first husband after a second marriage — a constraint on serial recombination that shaped subsequent Jewish marital law via the ketubah system.

↩ ◇ Ephrem the Syrian (365). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Deuteronomy (c. 365 AD)

On 'the Lord thy God is a consuming fire, even a jealous God' (Deu 4:24), Ephrem reads the doubled-image (consuming fire + jealous God) as the canonical Old-Testament anchor of Hebrews 12:29 ('for our God is a consuming fire' — verbatim citation). The fire-image is not destructive wrath but the purifying jealousy that refuses rival affections. Tewahedo theology cites Deu 4:24 + Heb 12:29 as the canonical doubled-witness that the encounter-with-God is always simultaneously consoling and consuming; the Eucharist itself receives the same description in the Tewahedo Anaphora of Athanasius: 'this is the burning coal which Isaiah saw'.

↩ ✦ Topic. Topics. This verse appears under: Fruit of, illustrative.

↩ ◇ Note. God as devouring fire. Paired with the immediate phrase following: "a jealous God." Hebrews 12:29 cites the verse directly: "our God is a consuming fire." The image is double-edged — fire is the warmth of presence and the danger of unmediated proximity. Deuteronomic theology insists on the otherness of God even within covenant intimacy.

↩ ⌘ Hebrew. The Shema. Sh’ma Yisrael, YHWH Eloheinu, YHWH eḥad. The most-recited verse in Jewish life, said morning and evening daily, and traditionally the last words on the lips of the dying. Jesus cites it (Mark 12:29) as the first commandment. The Hebrew eḥad ("one") is also the word for the unity of husband and wife (Gen 2:24) — relational unity, not just numerical. Christian tradition has read the verse Trinitarianly without abandoning monotheism by the same lexical move.

↩ ◇ Note. The motive of election. God did not choose Israel because they were great or many — he chose them because he chose them. The tautology of grace. The Deuteronomist returns to this theme repeatedly (10:15, 14:2, 23:5): election is grounded in love, not merit. Paul’s argument in Romans 9–11 about Israel’s election directly draws from this Deuteronomic theology.

↩ ◇ Ephrem the Syrian (365). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Deuteronomy (c. 365 AD)

On 'man doth not live by bread only, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of the Lord doth man live' (Deu 8:3), Ephrem reads the manna-pedagogy as the canonical anchor cited by Christ at the first Temptation (Mt 4:4 / Lk 4:4 — verbatim citation). The manna teaches that humanity's deepest hunger is for the Word, not for bread; the Eucharist resolves both hungers in one. Tewahedo eucharistic theology cites Deu 8:3 + Jn 6:51 ('I am the living bread which came down from heaven') + Mt 4:4 as the canonical triple-witness: Christ is the Word-who-is-Bread, fulfilling the Deuteronomic pedagogy in the Eucharistic anaphora.

↩ ✦ Topic. Topics. This verse appears under: Afflictions Made Beneficial, Afflictions Made Beneficial, Desert, Journey of Israel Through The, Desert, Journey of Israel Through The, Humility.

↩ ◇ Note. Cited at the Temptation. Jesus quotes this verse to Satan (Matt 4:4, Luke 4:4) when tempted to turn stones into bread after his forty-day fast — paralleling Israel’s forty years in the wilderness. The Deuteronomic point: the manna lesson was that life depends on God’s sustaining word, not just the substance of food. The wilderness was a school of dependence.

↩ ◇ Ephrem the Syrian (365). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Deuteronomy (c. 365 AD)

On 'Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart, and be no more stiffnecked' (Deu 10:16), Ephrem reads the heart-circumcision command as the canonical Old-Testament anchor of Paul's 'circumcision is that of the heart, in the spirit, and not in the letter' (Rom 2:29). The Deuteronomic call to interior circumcision is not a substitute for the bodily rite but its ground: the outward sign is empty without the inward reality. Tewahedo theology — uniquely among Christian communions still practising bodily circumcision per Jub 15:14-25 — cites Deu 10:16 as the canonical Old-Testament witness that BOTH circumcisions are required: the bodily sign that distinguishes the people and the heart-circumcision that perfects it.

↩ ◇ Note. Circumcision of the heart. The metaphor moves the covenantal sign from the body to the inner life. Jeremiah 4:4 develops it; Romans 2:28–29 lands the full Pauline reading: "a Jew is one inwardly, and circumcision is of the heart." The verse insists, already in the Mosaic law, that external sign without internal alignment is not enough.

↩ ◇ Ephrem the Syrian (365). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Deuteronomy (c. 365 AD)

On 'The Lord thy God will raise up unto thee a Prophet from the midst of thee, of thy brethren, like unto me; unto him ye shall hearken' (Deu 18:15), Ephrem reads the prophet-like-Moses promise as the canonical Old-Testament messianic anchor cited verbatim by Peter in Acts 3:22 ('A prophet shall the Lord your God raise up unto you of your brethren, like unto me') and by Stephen in Acts 7:37 — the apostolic preaching's primary Old-Testament prophecy-of-Christ proof-text alongside Ps 110:1. The 'like-Moses' qualification is fulfilled in Christ at the Transfiguration where Moses and Elijah appear with him on the mountain. Tewahedo christology cites Deu 18:15 + Acts 3:22 + the Buhe Transfiguration as the canonical triple-witness of the Mosaic-prophet identity of Christ.

↩ ◇ Ephrem the Syrian (365). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Deuteronomy (c. 365 AD)

On 'he that is hanged is accursed of God' (Deu 21:23), Ephrem reads the curse-on-the-hanged-corpse statute as the canonical Old-Testament anchor of Paul's atonement-formula in Galatians 3:13: 'Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us: for it is written, Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree' — verbatim citation. The Deuteronomic curse is not abolished but absorbed: Christ takes the curse upon himself precisely by hanging on the tree. Tewahedo atonement theology cites Deu 21:23 + Gal 3:13 as the canonical doubled-anchor of the substitutionary cross — the Cross is canonical-curse-bearing, the Christ is canonical-curse-bearer, the redemption is canonical-completion.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). CRUCIFIXION a common mode of punishment among heathen nations in early times. It is not certain whether it was known among the ancient Jews; probably it was not. The modes of capital punishment according to the Mosaic law were, by the sword (Exodus 21), strangling, fire (Leviticus 20), and stoning (Deuteronomy 21). This was regarded as the most horrible form of death, and to a Jew it would acquire greater horror from the curse in Deuteronomy 21:23. This punishment began by subjecting the sufferer to scourging. In the case of our Lord, however, his scourging was rather before the sentence was passed upon him, and was inflicted by Pilate for the purpose, probably, of exciting pity and procuring his escape from further punishment (Luke 23:22; John 19:1). The condemned one carried his own cross to the place of execution, which was outside the city, in some conspicuous place set apart for the purpose. Before the nailing to the cross took place, a medicated cup of vinegar mixed with gall and myrrh (the sopor) was given, for the purpose of deadening the pangs of the sufferer. Our Lord refused this cup, that his senses might be clear (Matthew 27:34). The spongeful of vinegar, sour wine, posca, the common drink of the Roman soldiers, which was put on a hyssop stalk and offered to our Lord in contemptuous pity (Matthew 27:48; Luke 23:36), he tasted to allay the agonies of his thirst (John 19:29). The accounts given of the crucifixion of our Lord are in entire agreement with the customs and practices of the Roman in such cases. He was crucified between two “malefactors” (Isaiah 53:12; Luke 23:32), and was watched by a party of four soldiers (John 19:23; Matthew 27:36, 54), with their centurion. The “breaking of the legs” of the malefactors was intended to hasten death, and put them out of misery (John 19:31); but the unusual rapidity of our Lord’s death (19:33) was due to his previous sufferings and his great mental anguish. The omission of the breaking of his legs was the fulfilment of a type (Exodus 12:46). He literally died of a broken heart, a ruptured heart, and hence the flowing of blood and water from the wound made by the soldier’s spear (John 19:34). Our Lord uttered seven memorable words from the cross, namely, (1) Luke 23:34; (2) 23:43; (3) John 19:26; (4) Matthew 27:46, Mark 15:34; (5) John 19:28; (6) 19:30; (7) Luke 23:46.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). HANGING (as a punishment), a mark of infamy inflicted on the dead bodies of criminals (Deuteronomy 21:23) rather than our modern mode of punishment. Criminals were first strangled and then hanged (Nu. 25:4; Deuteronomy 21:22). (See 2 Samuel 21:6 for the practice of the Gibeonites.) Hanging (as a curtain). (1.) Hebrews masak, (a) before the entrance to the court of the tabernacle (Exodus 35:17); (b) before the door of the tabernacle (26:36, 37); (c) before the entrance to the most holy place, called “the veil of the covering” (35:12; 39:34), as the word properly means. (2.) Hebrews kelaim, tapestry covering the walls of the tabernacle (Exodus 27:9; 35:17; Numbers 3:26) to the half of the height of the wall (Exodus 27:18; comp. 26:16). These hangings were fastened to pillars. (3.) Hebrews bottim (2 Kings 23:7), “hangings for the grove” (R.V., “for the Asherah”); marg., instead of “hangings,” has “tents” or “houses.” Such curtained structures for idolatrous worship are also alluded to in Ezekiel 16:16.

↩ ◇ Note. The hanged man cursed. Paul in Galatians 3:13 cites this verse — "cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree" — to interpret the crucifixion. The pre-Christian Jewish tradition had already extended the verse to crucifixion (4QpNah, on the Hasmonean crucifixions of Pharisees).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). ARNON swift, the southern boundary of the territory of Israel beyond Jordan, separating it from the land of Moab (Deuteronomy 3:8, 16). This river (referred to twenty-four times in the Bible) rises in the mountains of Gilead, and after a circuitous course of about 80 miles through a deep ravine it falls into the Dead Sea nearly opposite Engedi. The stream is almost dry in summer. It is now called el-Mujeb. The territory of the Amorites extended from the Arnon to the Jabbok.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). HERMON a peak, the eastern prolongation of the Anti-Lebanon range, reaching to the height of about 9,200 feet above the Mediterranean. It marks the north boundary of Palestine (Deuteronomy 3:8, 4:48; Joshua 11:3, 17; 13:11; 12:1), and is seen from a great distance. It is about 40 miles north of the Sea of Galilee. It is called “the Hermonites” (Psalm 42:6) because it has more than one summit. The Sidonians called it Sirion, and the Amorites Shenir (Deuteronomy 3:9; Cant. 4:8). It is also called Baal-hermon (Judges 3:3; 1 Chronicles 5:23) and Sion (Deuteronomy 4:48). There is every probability that one of its three summits was the scene of the transfiguration (q.v.). The “dew of Hermon” is referred to (Psalm 89: 12). Its modern name is Jebel-esh-Sheikh, “the chief mountain.” It is one of the most conspicuous mountains in Palestine or Syria. “In whatever part of Palestine the Israelite turned his eye northward, Hermon was there, terminating the view. From the plain along the coast, from the Jordan valley, from the heights of Moab and Gilead, from the plateau of Bashan, the pale, blue, snow-capped cone forms the one feature in the northern horizon.” Our Lord and his disciples climbed this “high mountain apart” one day, and remained on its summit all night, “weary after their long and toilsome ascent.” During the night “he was transfigured before them; and his face did shine as the sun.” The next day they descended to Caesarea Philippi.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). SENIR =Shenir, the name given to Hermon by the Amorites (Deuteronomy 3:9). It means “coat of mail” or “breastplate,” and is equivalent to “Sirion.” Some interpret the word as meaning “the prominent” or “the snowy mountain.” It is properly the name of the central of the three summits of Hermon (q.v.).

↩ ◇ Note. Og’s bed. The note about the iron bedstead — nine cubits long (about thirteen and a half feet) — is the OT’s most concrete giant-king detail and one of its few explicit cubit-measurements of an artifact. Some scholars (so Allen Millard) read the "iron bed" as a basaltic sarcophagus rather than a literal bed, since the volcanic basalt of the Bashan plateau resembles dark iron and was used for monumental burials in the region. Either way the verse functions as ANE-style royal trophy detail: the defeated king’s personal furniture, displayed in Ammonite Rabbah as material proof of his stature, becomes a touristic curiosity (the Hebrew "Isn’t it in Rabbah?" assumes the reader can verify). Og is identified as one of the Rephaim — the OT’s composite category for pre-Israelite giant-clans (cf. Gen 14:5, 15:20, Num 13:33, Deut 2:11) — and his defeat is one of the conquest-narrative’s headline accomplishments (cf. Ps 135:11, 136:20).

↩ ◇ Ephrem the Syrian (365). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Deuteronomy (c. 365 AD)

On the prologue to the Decalogue's restatement — 'I am the Lord thy God, which brought thee out of the land of Egypt, from the house of bondage' (Deu 5:6) — Ephrem reads the placement of the redemption-formula BEFORE the commandments as the canonical anchor of the order-of-salvation: grace precedes obligation, the Exodus precedes Sinai. The Decalogue is given to a people already redeemed, not to a people earning redemption. Tewahedo catechetical theology cites Deu 5:6 as the canonical Old-Testament anchor for the order baptism-precedes-commandments: the catechumen is delivered from Egypt (baptism) BEFORE receiving the Tewahedo moral-life formation.

↩ ◇ Note. The fifth commandment with promise. The Decalogue’s fifth commandment is the only one that attaches an explicit promise to the obligation — long days in the land. Eph 6:2–3 calls it "the first commandment with a promise," reading the linkage between obedience and durable life as theologically programmatic. The version here, in Deuteronomy’s second giving of the Decalogue, expands the Exod 20:12 form by adding the phrase "as Yahweh your God commanded you" (registering the prior Sinai promulgation) and the gloss "that it may go well with you" — characteristic Deuteronomistic enrichments. The commandment’s placement at the hinge between the Yahweh-directed first four and the human-directed last five (it concerns parents, but parents bearing a quasi-Yahweh role of authority and instruction) is theologically deliberate: family piety mediates between cult and ethics. Honoring parents in OT framing extends well into adult life and household-economic obligation, not just childhood obedience.

↩ ⌘ Hebrew. Shâmayim (שָׁמַיִם). the sky (as aloft; the dual perhaps alluding to the visible arch in which the clouds move, as well as to the higher ether where the celestial bodies revolve).

↩ ◇ Note. The anti-righteousness clause. Moses preempts the inevitable post-conquest interpretation that Israel possesses the land because Israel deserves it: the gift of the land is not Israel’s reward for moral worthiness but the displacement of the Canaanites for their wickedness combined with Yahweh’s prior promise to the patriarchs (9:5). The passage is theologically precise: Israel is given the land because of Canaanite iniquity and Abrahamic promise, not Israelite virtue — a triangulation that prevents both arrogance ("we earned this") and the theological problem of arbitrary divine favoritism. The chapter immediately reinforces this with the golden-calf retrospect (9:7–29): Israel is in fact a stiff-necked people, repeatedly forgiven through Mosaic intercession. Paul’s framing of Christian salvation in Eph 2:8–9 ("not by works, lest anyone should boast") draws on the same theological pattern — divine gift contingent on the giver’s purposes, not the recipient’s desert.

↩ ◇ Note. The cult-centralization principle. The chapter is the textual foundation of Deuteronomistic theology of worship: sacrifice and tithe must occur only at the one place Yahweh designates ("to put his name there"), in deliberate contrast to the multiple altars and high places implicit in earlier patriarchal practice (Gen 12:7–8, 13:18, 35:7) and explicit in the Israelite countryside well into the monarchic period (1 Kgs 22:43, "the high places were not removed"). Most modern OT scholarship (since W. M. L. de Wette, 1805) connects this chapter with the "book of the law" found during Josiah’s temple repair in 622 BCE (2 Kgs 22), which became the textual basis for Josiah’s centralization reforms (2 Kgs 23). On this reading, Deuteronomy 12 is the editorial heart of the seventh-century Yahwist program that produced Israel’s first sustained drive toward exclusive monolatrous worship at a single sanctuary — eventually fulfilled in the Jerusalem temple. The verse’s influence on subsequent biblical theology is hard to overstate: it shapes the Deuteronomistic critique of every later king and underwrites the post-exilic theology of Zion.

↩ ◇ Note. The closest possible enticement. The chapter triples the test of covenant loyalty against three levels of intimate enticement to apostasy: a prophet (13:1–5), a family member (13:6–11), and a whole town (13:12–18). The middle case is the most personally agonizing: a brother born of the same mother (closer than half-brother), or one’s wife "of your bosom," or a soul-friend secretly proposing other gods. The required Israelite response — execution, with the betrayed family member casting the first stone (13:9) — is shocking by modern measure and is presented that way in the text as well: Deuteronomy stages the cost of covenant exclusivity at maximum. Jesus’ saying that "anyone who comes to me and does not hate his father and mother… cannot be my disciple" (Luke 14:26) draws on this same Deuteronomic pattern of covenant claim above kinship. The chapter is one of the OT’s most uncompromising texts on the priority of religious fidelity over family bond, and one of the most theologically and ethically difficult.

↩ ◇ Note. The law of the king. Deuteronomy’s "law of the king" (17:14–20) anticipates Israelite monarchy and circumscribes it in advance: the king must be Yahweh-chosen, Israelite-born, must not multiply horses, wives, or silver, and must write his own copy of the Torah and read it daily. The text reads almost as a prosecutor’s indictment of Solomon retrojected centuries earlier — every prohibition listed (multiplying horses, wives, silver, returning to Egypt for trade) corresponds exactly to documented Solomonic violations (1 Kgs 10–11). Most scholars treat this as the deuteronomistic editor critiquing the monarchy through the literary device of Mosaic prophecy. The principle the law encodes — that political authority must remain Torah-subordinate, with the king studying the same Torah he is bound by — is one of the OT’s most institutionally creative limits on royal power, and it shapes the entire prophetic tradition’s critique of the kings.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). DIVORCE The dissolution of the marriage tie was regulated by the Mosaic law (Deuteronomy 24:1-4). The Jews, after the Captivity, were reguired to dismiss the foreign women they had married contrary to the law (Ezra 10:11-19). Christ limited the permission of divorce to the single case of adultery. It seems that it was not uncommon for the Jews at that time to dissolve the union on very slight pretences (Matthew 5:31, 32; 19:1-9; Mark 10:2-12; Luke 16:18). These precepts given by Christ regulate the law of divorce in the Christian Church.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). DEBTOR Various regulations as to the relation between debtor and creditor are laid down in the Scriptures. (1.) The debtor was to deliver up as a pledge to the creditor what he could most easily dispense with (Deuteronomy 24:10, 11). (2.) A mill, or millstone, or upper garment, when given as a pledge, could not be kept over night (Exodus 22:26, 27). (3.) A debt could not be exacted during the Sabbatic year (Deuteronomy 15:1-15). For other laws bearing on this relation see Leviticus 25:14, 32, 39; Matthew 18:25, 34. (4.) A surety was liable in the same way as the original debtor (Proverbs 11:15; 17:18).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). KNOCK “Though Orientals are very jealous of their privacy, they never knock when about to enter your room, but walk in without warning or ceremony. It is nearly impossible to teach an Arab servant to knock at your door. They give warning at the outer gate either by calling or knocking. To stand and call is a very common and respectful mode. Thus Moses commanded the holder of a pledge to stand without and call to the owner to come forth (Deuteronomy 24:10). This was to avoid the violent intrusion of cruel creditors. Peter stood knocking at the outer door (Acts 12:13, 16), and the three men sent to Joppa by Cornelius made inquiry and ‘stood before the gate’ (10:17, 18). The idea is that the guard over your privacy is to be placed at the entrance.” Knocking is used as a sign of importunity (Matthew 7:7, 8; Luke 13:25), and of the coming of Christ (Luke 12:36; Revelation 3:20).

↩ ◇ Note. Individual responsibility. The verse establishes the principle that judicial death is individual: the executioner cannot kill the criminal’s family in his place, nor extend punishment to the next generation. The ruling stands in tension with other OT texts that affirm intergenerational consequence (Exod 20:5, "visiting iniquity to the third and fourth generation"; 2 Sam 21, the seven Saulide grandsons executed for Saul’s violation of the Gibeonite oath). Ezekiel’s extended treatise on individual responsibility (Ezek 18) explicitly cites this principle and extends it programmatically. 2 Kgs 14:6 records King Amaziah obeying the verse — refusing to execute the children of his father’s assassins — and the deuteronomistic editor highlights the obedience approvingly. The verse is one of the foundational texts in the OT’s gradual development from collective-clan responsibility (the older norm in ANE legal traditions) toward individual judicial accountability. Modern criminal-law principles of personal responsibility descend from this development.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). CUTTING the flesh in various ways was an idolatrous practice, a part of idol-worship (Deuteronomy 14:1; 1 Kings 18:28). The Israelites were commanded not to imitate this practice (Leviticus 19:28; 21:5; Deuteronomy 14:1). The tearing of the flesh from grief and anguish of spirit in mourning for the dead was regarded as a mark of affection (Jeremiah 16:6; 41:5; 48:37). Allusions are made in Revelation (13:16; 17:5; 19:20) to the practice of printing marks on the body, to indicate allegiance to a deity. We find also references to it, through in a different direction, by Paul (Galatians 6; 7) and by Ezekiel (9:4). (See HAIR.)

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). CHAMOIS only in Deuteronomy 14:5 (Hebrews zemer), an animal of the deer or gazelle species. It bears this Hebrew name from its leaping or springing. The animal intended is probably the wild sheep (Ovis tragelephus), which is still found in Sinai and in the broken ridges of Stony Arabia. The LXX. and Vulgate render the word by camelopardus, i.e., the giraffe; but this is an animal of Central Africa, and is not at all known in Syria.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). FALLOW-DEER Deuteronomy 14:5 (R.V., “Wild goat”); 1 Kings 4:23 (R.V., “roebucks”). This animal, called in Hebrew yahmur, from a word meaning “to be red,” is regarded by some as the common fallow-deer, the Cervus dama, which is said to be found very generally over Western and Southern Asia. It is called “fallow” from its pale-red or yellow colour. Some interpreters, however, regard the name as designating the bubale, Antelope bubale, the “wild cow” of North Africa, which is about the size of a stag, like the hartebeest of South Africa. A species of deer has been found at Mount Carmel which is called yahmur by the Arabs. It is said to be similar to the European roebuck.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). PYGARG Hebrews dishon, “springing”, (Deuteronomy 14:5), one of the animals permitted for food. It is supposed to be the Antelope addax. It is described as “a large animal, over 3 1/2 feet high at the shoulder, and, with its gently-twisted horns, 2 1/2 feet long. Its colour is pure white, with the exception of a short black mane, and a tinge of tawny on the shoulders and back.”, Tristram’s Natural History. Q

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). ROE (Hebrews tsebi), properly the gazelle (Arab. ghazal), permitted for food (Deuteronomy 14:5; comp. Deuteronomy 12:15, 22; 15:22; 1 Kings 4:23), noted for its swiftness and beauty and grace of form (2 Samuel 2:18; 1 Chronicles 12:8; Cant. 2:9; 7:3; 8:14). The gazelle (Gazella dorcas) is found in great numbers in Palestine. “Among the gray hills of Galilee it is still ‘the roe upon the mountains of Bether,’ and I have seen a little troop of gazelles feeding on the Mount of Olives close to Jerusalem itself” (Tristram). The Hebrew word (‘ayyalah) in Proverbs 5: 19 thus rendered (R.V., “doe”), is properly the “wild she-goat,” the mountain goat, the ibex. (See 1 Samuel 24:2; Psalm 104:18; Job 39:1.)

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). GLEDE an Old English name for the common kite, mentioned only in Deuteronomy 14:13 (Hebrews ra’ah), the Milvus ater or black kite. The Hebrew word does not occur in the parallel passage in Leviticus (11:14, da’ah, rendered “vulture;” in R.V., “kite”). It was an unclean bird. The Hebrew name is from a root meaning “to see,” “to look,” thus designating a bird with a keen sight. The bird intended is probably the buzzard, of which there are three species found in Palestine. (See VULTURE.)

↩ ⌘ Hebrew. Lo t’vashshel g’di ba-ḥalev immo (לֹא־תְבַשֵּׁל גְּדִי בַּחֲלֵב אִמּוֹ). The prohibition appears three times in the Pentateuch (here, Exod 23:19, Exod 34:26) — a textual triple-attestation that, in rabbinic interpretation (b. Hullin 113b), generates the threefold separation of meat from milk in kashrut: not cooking together, not eating together, not benefiting from the mixture. The literal practice the verse forbids is documented in the 14th-century-BCE Ugaritic ritual texts (KTU 1.23, the "Birth of the Gracious Gods"), where boiling a kid in milk appears as a Canaanite ritual gesture — making the verse a pointed prohibition of a specific known pagan rite. The rabbinic generalization is therefore an interpretive expansion well beyond the literal sense, but the literal sense itself is precisely calibrated: avoid the cultic practice of the surrounding peoples. The verse is one of the OT’s most striking examples of how a single ritual prohibition can generate an entire dietary tradition.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). DIZAHAB region of gold, a place in the desert of Sinai, on the western shore of the Elanitic gulf (Deuteronomy 1:1). It is now called Dehab.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). LABAN white. (1.) The son of Bethuel, who was the son of Nahor, Abraham’s brother. He lived at Haran in Mesopotamia. His sister Rebekah was Isaac’s wife (Genesis 24). Jacob, one of the sons of this marriage, fled to the house of Laban, whose daughters Leah and Rachel (ch. 29) he eventually married. (See JACOB.) (2.) A city in the Arabian desert in the route of the Israelites (Deuteronomy 1:1), probably identical with Libnah (Numbers 33:20).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). SUPH (Deuteronomy 1:1, R.V.; marg., “some ancient versions have the Red Sea,” as in the A.V.). Some identify it with Suphah (Numbers 21:14, marg., A.V.) as probably the name of a place. Others identify it with es-Sufah = Maaleh-acrabbim (Joshua 15:3), and others again with Zuph (1 Samuel 9:5). It is most probable, however, that, in accordance with the ancient versions, this word is to be regarded as simply an abbreviation of Yam-suph, i.e., the “Red Sea.”

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). TOPHEL lime, a place in the wilderness of Sinai (Deuteronomy 1:1), now identified with Tafyleh or Tufileh, on the west side of the Edomitish mountains.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). ASHTAROTH a city of Bashan, in the kingdom of Og (Deuteronomy 1:4; Joshua 12:4; 13:12; 9:10). It was in the half-tribe of Manasseh (Joshua 13:12), and as a Levitical city was given to the Gershonites (1 Chronicles 6:71). Uzzia, one of David’s valiant men (1 Chronicles 11:44), is named as of this city. It is identified with Tell Ashterah, in the Hauran, and is noticed on monuments B.C. 1700-1500. The name Beesh-terah (Joshua 21:27) is a contraction for Beth-eshterah, i.e., “the house of Ashtaroth.”

FATHER a name applied (1) to any ancestor (Deuteronomy 1:11; 1 Kings 15:11; Matthew 3:9; 23:30, etc.); and (2) as a title of respect to a chief, ruler, or elder, etc. (Judges 17:10; 18:19; 1 Samuel 10:12; 2 Kings 2:12; Matthew 23:9, etc.). (3) The author or beginner of anything is also so called; e.g., Jabal and Jubal (Genesis 4:20, 21; comp. Job 38:28). Applied to God (Exodus 4:22; Deuteronomy 32:6; 2 Samuel 7:14; Psalm 89:27, 28, etc.). (1.) As denoting his covenant relation to the Jews (Jeremiah 31:9; Isaiah 63:16; 64:8; John 8:41, etc.). (2.) Believers are called God’s “sons” (John 1:12; Romans 8:16; Matthew 6:4, 8, 15, 18; 10:20, 29). They also call him “Father” (Romans 1:7; 1 Corinthians 1:3; 2 Corinthians 1:2; Galatians 1:4)

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). MAGISTRATE a public civil officer invested with authority. The Hebrew shophetim, or judges, were magistrates having authority in the land (Deuteronomy 1:16, 17). In Judges 18:7 the word “magistrate” (A.V.) is rendered in the Revised Version “possessing authority”, i.e., having power to do them harm by invasion. In the time of Ezra (9:2) and Nehemiah (2:16; 4:14; 13:11) the Jewish magistrates were called seganim, properly meaning “nobles.” In the New Testament the Greek word archon, rendered “magistrate” (Luke 12:58; Titus 3:1), means one first in power, and hence a prince, as in Matthew 20:25, 1 Corinthians 2:6, 8. This term is used of the Messiah, “Prince of the kings of the earth” (Revelation 1:5). In Acts 16:20, 22, 35, 36, 38, the Greek term strategos, rendered “magistrate,” properly signifies the leader of an army, a general, one having military authority. The strategoi were the duumviri, the two praetors appointed to preside over the administration of justice in the colonies of the Romans. They were attended by the sergeants (properly lictors or “rod bearers”).

↩ ◇ Note. Yahweh the parent. The simile is one of the OT’s most affecting parental images for Yahweh — not the father-as-disciplinarian familiar from royal-adoption language (cf. 2 Sam 7:14, Ps 2:7) but the father-as-bearer, the parent who literally carries the dependent child through difficult terrain. The same image returns at Deut 32:11 (the eagle bearing its young), Hos 11:3 ("I taught Ephraim to walk; I took them up by their arms"), and Isa 46:3–4 ("you have been borne by me from before your birth… even to your old age I am he"). The cluster of texts forms one of the OT’s richest theological strains: divine fidelity as parental endurance through the long span of a child’s helplessness. The image is conspicuously gendered both ways — Yahweh as father (here, Hos 11) and as nursing mother (Isa 49:15, 66:13) — registering the deity beyond the gender categories of human parenting.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). ELATH grove; trees, (Deuteronomy 2:8), also in plural form Eloth (1 Kings 9:26, etc.); called by the Greeks and Romans Elana; a city of Idumea, on the east, i.e., the Elanitic, gulf, or the Gulf of Akabah, of the Red Sea. It is first mentioned in Deuteronomy 2:8. It is also mentioned along with Ezion-geber in 1 Kings 9:26. It was within the limits of Solomon’s dominion, but afterwards revolted. It was, however, recovered and held for a time under king Uzziah (2 Kings 14:22). Now the ruin Aila.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). ZAMZUMMIMS a race of giants; “a people great, and many, and tall, as the Anakims” (Deuteronomy 2:20, 21). They were overcome by the Ammonites, “who called them Zamzummims.” They belonged to the Rephaim, and inhabited the country afterwards occupied by the Ammonites. It has been conjectured that they might be Ham-zuzims, i.e., Zuzims dwelling in Ham, a place apparently to the south of Ashteroth (Genesis 14:5), the ancient Rabbath-ammon.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). AVIM a people dwelling in Hazerim, or “the villages” or “encampments” on the south-west corner of the sea-coast (Deuteronomy 2:23). They were subdued and driven northward by the Caphtorim. A trace of them is afterwards found in Joshua 13:3, where they are called Avites.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). CAPHTOR a chaplet, the original seat of the Philistines (Deuteronomy 2:23; Jeremiah 47:4; Amos 9:7). The name is found written in hieroglyphics in the temple of Kom Ombos in Upper Egypt. But the exact situation of Caphtor is unknown, though it is supposed to be Crete, since the Philistines seem to be meant by the “Cherethites” in 1 Samuel 30:14 (see also 2 Samuel 8:18). It may, however, have been a part of Egypt, the Caphtur in the north Delta, since the Caphtorim were of the same race as the Mizraite people (Genesis 10:14; 1 Chronicles 1:12).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). GAZA called also Azzah, which is its Hebrew name (Deuteronomy 2:23; 1 Kings 4:24; Jeremiah 25:20), strong, a city on the Mediterranean shore, remarkable for its early importance as the chief centre of a great commercial traffic with Egypt. It is one of the oldest cities of the world (Genesis 10:19; Joshua 15:47). Its earliest inhabitants were the Avims, who were conquered and displaced by the Caphtorims (Deuteronomy 2:23; Joshua 13:2, 3), a Philistine tribe. In the division of the land it fell to the lot of Judah (Joshua 15:47; Judges 1:18). It was the southernmost of the five great Philistine cities which gave each a golden emerod as a trespass-offering unto the Lord (1 Samuel 6:17). Its gates were carried away by Samson (Judges 16:1-3). Here he was afterwards a prisoner, and “did grind in the prison house.” Here he also pulled down the temple of Dagon, and slew “all the lords of the Philistines,” himself also perishing in the ruin (Judges 16:21-30). The prophets denounce the judgments of God against it (Jeremiah 25:20; 47:5; Amos 1:6, 7; Zephaniah 2:4). It is referred to in Acts 8:26. Philip is here told to take the road from Jerusalem to Gaza (about 6 miles south-west of Jerusalem), “which is desert”, i.e., the “desert road,” probably by Hebron, through the desert hills of Southern Judea. (See SAMSON.) It is noticed on monuments as early as B.C. 1600. Its small port is now called el-Mineh.

↩ ◇ Note. The hardened heart problem. Sihon’s refusal to allow Israelite passage is attributed directly to Yahweh’s hardening of his spirit — the same theological language used of Pharaoh in Exod 4:21, 7:3, 9:12, etc. The pattern raises the OT’s most persistent moral-theological tension: divine sovereignty over human refusal that nonetheless remains accountable as refusal. The Pharaoh narratives carefully alternate "Pharaoh hardened his heart" and "Yahweh hardened Pharaoh’s heart" formulas; here Deuteronomy collapses the distinction toward the divine causation. Paul’s extended discussion in Rom 9:14–24 (citing Exod 9:16 directly) is the NT’s most sustained engagement with this theological problem. Augustine, Calvin, and Aquinas read the passages differently — but the textual phenomenon Paul is grappling with begins at verses like this one, where divine causation and human responsibility are affirmed simultaneously without the OT showing any felt need to systematize the apparent tension.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). ENTERTAIN Entertainments, “feasts,” were sometimes connected with a public festival (Deuteronomy 16:11, 14), and accompanied by offerings (1 Samuel 9:13), in token of alliances (Genesis 26:30); sometimes in connection with domestic or social events, as at the weaning of children (Genesis 21:8), at weddings (Genesis 29:22; John 2:1), on birth-days (Matthew 14:6), at the time of sheep-shearing (2 Samuel 13:23), and of vintage (Judges 9:27), and at funerals (2 Samuel 3:35; Jeremiah 16:7). The guests were invited by servants (Proverbs 9:3; Matthew 22:3), who assigned them their respective places (1 Samuel 9:22; Luke 14:8; Mark 12:39). Like portions were sent by the master to each guest (1 Samuel 1:4; 2 Samuel 6:19), except when special honour was intended, when the portion was increased (Genesis 43:34). The Israelites were forbidden to attend heathenish sacrificial entertainments (Exodus 34:15), because these were in honour of false gods, and because at such feast they would be liable to partake of unclean flesh (1 Corinthians 10:28). In the entertainments common in apostolic times among the Gentiles were frequent “revellings,” against which Christians were warned (Romans 13:13; Galatians 5:21; 1 Peter 4:3). (See BANQUET.)

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). DEGREES , SONG OF song of steps, a title given to each of these fifteen psalms, 120-134 inclusive. The probable origin of this name is the circumstance that these psalms came to be sung by the people on the ascents or goings up to Jerusalem to attend the three great festivals (Deuteronomy 16:16). They were well fitted for being sung by the way from their peculiar form, and from the sentiments they express. “They are characterized by brevity, by a key-word, by epanaphora [i.e, repetition], and by their epigrammatic style...More than half of them are cheerful, and all of them hopeful.” They are sometimes called “Pilgrim Songs.” Four of them were written by David, one (127) by Solomon, and the rest are anonymous.

↩ ◇ Note. The Israelite court system. The verse institutes a tribal judicial structure — judges (shofetim) and officers (shoterim, likely court-marshals or enforcement officers) at every city gate. The "gate" was the OT’s standard public legal venue (Ruth 4:1–11, Boaz’s court case; Amos 5:10, "they hate him who reproves in the gate"; Job 29:7, the patriarch’s public seat at the gate). Archaeological work at Iron Age Israelite city-gates (Tel Dan, Beersheba, Gezer) has revealed bench-lined gate-chambers consistent with this judicial-administrative function. The chapter’s next verses (16:19–20) prohibit bribery and partiality and famously command "Justice, justice (tzedek tzedek) you shall pursue" — the doubled noun is one of the OT’s most cited rhetorical intensifiers. The verse establishes the institutional framework for Israelite local justice that operates throughout the monarchic period.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). STRANGER This word generally denotes a person from a foreign land residing in Palestine. Such persons enjoyed many privileges in common with the Jews, but still were separate from them. The relation of the Jews to strangers was regulated by special laws (Deuteronomy 23:3; 24:14-21; 25:5; 26:10-13). A special signification is also sometimes attached to this word. In Genesis 23:4 it denotes one resident in a foreign land; Exodus 23:9, one who is not a Jew; Numbers 3:10, one who is not of the family of Aaron; Psalm 69:8, an alien or an unknown person. The Jews were allowed to purchase strangers as slaves (Leviticus 25:44, 45), and to take usury from them (Deuteronomy 23:20).

↩ ◇ Note. The interest prohibition. The verse forbids lending at interest to a fellow Israelite (cf. Exod 22:25, Lev 25:35–37) while permitting it to foreigners (23:20). The asymmetry encodes a specifically covenantal economic ethic: financial gain from a brother’s misfortune is prohibited, but participation in the wider commercial credit economy is permitted. The verse becomes the textual ground for Christian and Jewish anti-usury traditions (medieval canon law, the rabbinic halakhic debates over ribbit, the Church’s Lateran prohibitions) and indirectly for the historical limitation of Jewish economic life to lending professions in medieval Europe (Christians forbidding usury internally created the niche). Modern Islamic finance (the prohibition of riba) descends from the same tradition. The verse is one of the OT’s most economically consequential texts, generating two and a half millennia of legal-religious adaptation.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). MEAT-OFFERING (Hebrews minhah), originally a gift of any kind. This Hebrew word came latterly to denote an “unbloody” sacrifice, as opposed to a “bloody” sacrifice. A “drink-offering” generally accompanied it. The law regarding it is given in Leviticus 2, and 6:14-23. It was a recognition of the sovereignty of God and of his bounty in giving all earthly blessings (1 Chronicles 29:10-14; Deuteronomy 26:5-11). It was an offering which took for granted and was based on the offering for sin. It followed the sacrifice of blood. It was presented every day with the burnt-offering (Exodus 29:40, 41), and consisted of flour or of cakes prepared in a special way with oil and frankincense.

↩ ◇ Note. The first-fruits confession. The chapter prescribes a liturgical recitation accompanying the offering of first-fruits — the so-called "Wandering Aramean" creed (26:5–10) — and verse 8 is the credal core. The text is the OT’s clearest example of a fixed liturgical confession: Israel must say specific words ("a wandering Aramean was my father…"), not just bring the offering. Most OT scholarship since Gerhard von Rad’s "The Form-Critical Problem of the Hexateuch" (1938) treats this confession as one of the oldest credal kernels of Israelite faith — possibly preserving pre-monarchic liturgical tradition. The phrase "with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm" recurs across the Pentateuch (Exod 6:6, Deut 4:34, 5:15, 26:8, Ps 136:12) as Israel’s standard exodus-formula, and it enters the Passover Haggadah essentially verbatim. The verse is the textual root of Jewish liturgical historical confession that descends through the Haggadah to modern Passover practice.

↩ ◇ Note. The Levites’ liturgical curses. The chapter stages a covenant-renewal ceremony on entering the land: half the tribes on Mount Gerizim recite the blessings, half on Mount Ebal recite the curses, with the Levites pronouncing twelve specific anathemas (27:15–26) to which the people respond "Amen." The format is theologically precise — covenants in the ANE typically included blessings and curses (Hittite vassal treaties, the Sefire inscriptions); the OT’s innovation is the antiphonal liturgical staging with named geography. The twelve curses cover idolatry (27:15), parental dishonor (16), social-economic abuse of the vulnerable (17–19), forbidden sexual relations (20–23), homicide and judicial bribery (24–25), and a comprehensive closing curse (26, "cursed is he who does not confirm the words of this law to do them" — the verse Paul will weaponize in Gal 3:10). The chapter is one of the OT’s clearest demonstrations that covenant is liturgical event, not just text.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). RABBAH or Rab’bath, great. (1.) “Rabbath of the children of Ammon,” the chief city of the Ammonites, among the eastern hills, some 20 miles east of the Jordan, on the southern of the two streams which united with the Jabbok. Here the bedstead of Og was preserved (Deuteronomy 3:11), perhaps as a trophy of some victory gained by the Ammonites over the king of Bashan. After David had subdued all their allies in a great war, he sent Joab with a strong force to take their city. For two years it held out against its assailants. It was while his army was engaged in this protracted siege that David was guilty of that deed of shame which left a blot on his character and cast a gloom over the rest of his life. At length, having taken the “royal city” (or the “city of waters,” 2 Samuel 12:27, i.e., the lower city on the river, as distinguished from the citadel), Joab sent for David to direct the final assault (11:1; 12:26-31). The city was given up to plunder, and the people were ruthlessly put to death, and “thus did he with all the cities of the children of Ammon.” The destruction of Rabbath was the last of David’s conquests. His kingdom now reached its farthest limits (2 Samuel 8:1-15; 1 Chronicles 18:1-15). The capture of this city is referred to by Amos (1:14), Jeremiah (49:2, 3), and Ezekiel (21:20; 25:5). (2.) A city in the hill country of Judah (Joshua 15:60), possibly the ruin Rubba, six miles north-east of Beit-Jibrin.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). CHINNERETH lyre, the singular form of the word (Deuteronomy 3:17; Joshua 19:35), which is also used in the plural form, Chinneroth, the name of a fenced city which stood near the shore of the lake of Galilee, a little to the south of Tiberias. The town seems to have given its name to a district, as appears from 1 Kings 15:20, where the plural form of the word is used. The Sea of Chinnereth (Numbers 34:11; Joshua 13:27), or of Chinneroth (Joshua 12: 3), was the “lake of Gennesaret” or “sea of Tiberias” (Deuteronomy 3:17; Joshua 11:2). Chinnereth was probably an ancient Canaanitish name adopted by the Israelites into their language.

↩ ◇ Note. The rhetorical-monolatrous question. Moses’ prayer poses the question — what god in heaven or earth can do such works as Yahweh? — in a form that does not categorically deny other gods’ existence but asserts Yahweh’s incomparable power among them. The construction is characteristic of Israelite monolatrous theology in its earlier strata: the existence of the surrounding pantheon is acknowledged or left untouched, while Yahweh’s practical supremacy is asserted (compare Exod 15:11, "Who is like you, Yahweh, among the gods?"; Ps 86:8, 89:6). The fully developed monotheistic claim — that other gods do not exist at all — emerges most clearly in Second Isaiah (Isa 44:6, 45:5–6, 18). The verse is one of many that show the OT theological development from monolatry (one Yahweh among real gods) toward strict monotheism (Yahweh alone is real) as a long process internal to the canon, not a single moment.

↩ ◇ Note. The wilderness-rebellion catalog. The chapter rehearses Israel’s wilderness failures — the golden calf at Horeb (9:8–21), the rebellion at Taberah, Massah, Kibroth-hattaavah (9:22), and the refusal to enter the land at Kadesh-barnea (9:23). The rhetorical function is preventive: Moses recites the failures so that Israel cannot, on entering the land, mistake survival for moral worthiness. The same pattern of wilderness-rebellion recital recurs at Pss 78, 95, 106, and Ezek 20 — each generation re-tells the failures to prevent its own. The Christian Letter to the Hebrews (Heb 3:7–4:11) extends the pattern to the church: the wilderness rebellion is the warning case for any community in covenant relationship with Yahweh. The verse is a structural pillar of the OT’s wisdom-by-failure pedagogy, where Israel’s religious instruction proceeds primarily by remembered catastrophe rather than abstract precept.

↩ ◇ Ephrem the Syrian (365). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Deuteronomy (c. 365 AD)

On 'the place which the Lord your God shall choose out of all your tribes to put his name there' (Deu 12:5), Ephrem reads the centralization-of-worship command as the canonical Old-Testament typological anchor that flows through Shiloh → Jerusalem → Zion → the Eucharistic altar of every local church. The Lord chooses ONE place for his Name in the Old Covenant; in the New Covenant, every Eucharistic altar is THE chosen place because the Body broken there IS the New-Covenant tabot. Tewahedo eucharistic theology cites Deu 12:5 as the canonical anchor for the doctrine that the Eucharist gathers Jerusalem's centralization into every parish — the tabot-bearing altar IS the chosen place.

↩ ◇ Note. Profane slaughter. The verse marks one of Deuteronomy’s most consequential legal innovations: the desacralization of ordinary meat-eating. Earlier Pentateuchal law (Lev 17:3–4) treated all animal slaughter as cultic — every killing of an animal had to be brought to the sanctuary as a peace-offering, with the blood disposed of properly. Deuteronomy, anticipating cult centralization at one distant sanctuary, makes ordinary slaughter for food permitted "in all your gates" — within any town — provided the blood is poured out (12:16). The legal change is enormous: meat consumption is partially uncoupled from sacrifice, and a distinction between sacred and ordinary slaughter enters Israelite practice for the first time. Most scholars treat this provision as one of the strongest internal indicators that Deuteronomy was composed (or radically edited) during the seventh-century push toward Jerusalem-centric worship, when the practical impossibility of bringing every animal to one sanctuary required a legal accommodation. The verse quietly transforms how Israelites actually ate.

↩ ⌘ Hebrew. Am s’gullah (עַם סְגֻלָּה). "A treasured people" — the term s’gullah means a personal treasure, the kind a king might keep separately from the public treasury. The same term describes Israel in Exod 19:5, Deut 7:6, 26:18, and Mal 3:17 (where the righteous are Yahweh’s s’gullah "in the day that I make"). The Christian appropriation of the term — 1 Pet 2:9, "a people for his own possession" — applies the formula to the Church, with conscious dependence on the Septuagint Greek (laos eis peripoiēsin). The verse encodes Israel’s self-understanding as the deity’s personal portion among the nations — a status that is theologically positive (covenant election) and practically demanding (the dietary and ritual distinctiveness the chapter goes on to detail). The chosen-people theology has had a long and complicated history; the OT itself uses the term for both blessing and obligation simultaneously.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). MOUNT Palestine is a hilly country (Deuteronomy 3:25; 11:11; Ezekiel 34:13). West of Jordan the mountains stretch from Lebanon far down into Galilee, terminating in Carmel. The isolated peak of Tabor rises from the elevated plain of Esdraelon, which, in the south, is shut in by hills spreading over the greater part of Samaria. The mountains of Western and Middle Palestine do not extend to the sea, but gently slope into plains, and toward the Jordan fall down into the Ghor. East of the Jordan the Anti-Lebanon, stretching south, terminates in the hilly district called Jebel Heish, which reaches down to the Sea of Gennesareth. South of the river Hieromax there is again a succession of hills, which are traversed by wadies running toward the Jordan. These gradually descend to a level at the river Arnon, which was the boundary of the ancient trans-Jordanic territory toward the south. The composition of the Palestinian hills is limestone, with occasional strata of chalk, and hence the numerous caves, some of large extent, found there.

↩ ✦ Topic. Topics. This verse appears under: Holy Land, Lebanon, Lebanon, Mountains.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). ABARIM regions beyond; i.e., on the east of Jordan, a mountain, or rather a mountain-chain, over against Jericho, to the east and south-east of the Dead Sea, in the land of Moab. From “the top of Pisgah”, i.e., Mount Nebo (q.v.), one of its summits, Moses surveyed the Promised Land (Deuteronomy 3:27; 32:49), and there he died (34:1,5). The Israelites had one of their encampments in the mountains of Abarim (Numbers 33:47,48) after crossing the Arnon.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). NORTHWARD (Hebrews tsaphon), a “hidden” or “dark place,” as opposed to the sunny south (Deuteronomy 3:27). A Hebrew in speaking of the points of the compass was considered as always having his face to the east, and hence “the left hand” (Genesis 14:15; Job 23:9) denotes the north. The “kingdoms of the north” are Chaldea, Assyria, Media, etc.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). WESTWARD sea-ward, i.e., toward the Mediterranean (Deuteronomy 3:27).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). GOLAN exile, a city of Bashan (Deuteronomy 4:43), one of the three cities of refuge east of Jordan, about 12 miles north-east of the Sea of Galilee (Joshua 20:8). There are no further notices of it in Scripture. It became the head of the province of Gaulanitis, one of the four provinces into which Bashan was divided after the Babylonish captivity, and almost identical with the modern Jaulan, in Western Hauran, about 39 miles in length and 18 in breath.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). RAMOTH-GILEAD heights of Gilead, a city of refuge on the east of Jordan; called “Ramoth in Gilead” (Deuteronomy 4:43; Joshua 20:8; 21:38). Here Ahab, who joined Jehoshaphat in an endeavour to rescue it from the hands of the king of Syria, was mortally wounded (1 Kings 22:1-36). A similar attempt was afterwards made by Ahaziah and Joram, when the latter was wounded (2 Kings 8:28). In this city Jehu, the son of Jehoshaphat, was anointed by one of the sons of the prophets (9:1, 4). It has with probability been identified with Reimun, on the northern slope of the Jabbok, about 5 miles west of Jerash or Gerasa, one of the cities of Decapolis. Others identify it with Gerosh, about 25 miles north-east of es-Salt, with which also many have identified it. (See RAMATH-MIZPEH.)
